subject: physics
question_text: If the temperature is measured in Fahrenheit instead of Celsius, does the value of the coefficient of expansion of a solid change? Explain.

mark_split.label: The relation between the two values

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 11 Very Short Answer Question 3 (printed p.116). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: a coefficient of expansion is a change in size per unit rise of temperature, and a Fahrenheit degree is 5/9 the size of a Celsius degree, so the same physical expansion gives a smaller number when expressed per Fahrenheit degree: α(per °F) = (5/9) × α(per °C). The physical expansion itself does not depend on the scale used to measure it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Yes, it changes
lines: A coefficient of expansion is a change
per degree, and a Fahrenheit degree is
steps.margin_note: First mark. Yes, together with the reason.
steps.why: A coefficient of expansion states how much the size changes for a one-degree rise, so its number depends on the size of the degree used to measure it.
common_mistakes: Answering no. The physical expansion is unchanged, but the number describing it per degree is not.
Saying a Fahrenheit degree is larger than a Celsius degree. It is smaller.

recall.must_convey: That yes, the value changes, because a Fahrenheit degree is a smaller unit of temperature than a Celsius degree.
accept: value depends on the size of the degree
reject: five ninths times alpha per Celsius

steps.memory_tip: The expansion itself does not change. Only the number changes with the size of the degree.

steps.label: The relation between the two values
lines: A Fahrenheit degree is 5/9 the size
of a Celsius degree, so the same
expansion gives a smaller number in °F.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write the 5/9 relation between the two values.
steps.why: A Fahrenheit degree is smaller than a Celsius degree, so a temperature rise of one Fahrenheit degree is a smaller rise, and the expansion measured per Fahrenheit degree is smaller by that same factor, 5/9.
common_mistakes: Writing the factor as 9/5 instead of 5/9, which reverses which value is larger.

recall.must_convey: That α(per °F) = (5/9) × α(per °C), because a Fahrenheit degree is the smaller unit.
accept: five ninths times alpha per Celsius
alpha per Fahrenheit equals five ninths

steps.memory_tip: Five ninths — the same fraction that turns a Celsius reading into Fahrenheit degrees.

insider_note: Two marks — the word yes with the reason, then the relation α(per °F) = (5/9) × α(per °C). Reversing the fraction is the common slip.
